claim: Kindlin-3 is expressed in CD4/CD8 double negative (DN) and double positive (DP) T cells from wild-type thymi and SP CD4 and CD8 T cells from WT spleens.
source: Kindlin-3 is expressed in CD4/CD8 double negative (DN) and double positive (DP) T cells from wild-type (WT) thymi and SP CD4 and CD8 T cells from WT spleens (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A demonstrating kindlin-3 protein expression in sorted T cell populations.

claim: Fermt3-/- mice die of severe bleedings and anemia within the first week after birth.
source: To test whether kindlin-3 expression is required for thymopoiesis, we investigated thymus morphology and size in kindlin-3-deficient (Fermt3-/-) mice, which die of severe bleedings and anemia within the first week after birth (Moser et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous publication (Moser et al., 2008).

claim: The morphology of Fermt3-/- thymi was normal and the size steadily increased until postnatal day 3.
source: The morphology of Fermt3-/- thymi was normal and the size steadily increased until postnatal day (P) 3 (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by images and measurements shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: While WT thymi continued to grow postnatally, Fermt3-/- thymi shrank and became atrophic.
source: However, while WT thymi continued to grow postnatally, Fermt3-/- thymi shrank and became atrophic (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by images in Figure 1B showing progressive thymus atrophy in Fermt3-/- mice after P3.

claim: The cellularity of WT thymi continuously increased during development.
source: Consistently, the cellularity of WT thymi continuously increased during development (Figure 1C)
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 1C showing increasing thymocyte numbers in WT mice from E14.5 to P8.

claim: Fermt3-/- thymi showed an increase in cellularity only until P3, followed by a dramatic decrease at P6 and P8.
source: while Fermt3-/- thymi showed an increase in cellularity only until P3, followed by a dramatic decrease at P6 and P8 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 1C showing thymocyte numbers in Fermt3-/- mice peaking at P3 and declining thereafter.

claim: The number of cells was significantly lower in Fermt3-/- thymi compared to controls at all time points analyzed.
source: Despite the progressive increase in cellularity until P3 the number of cells was significantly lower in Fermt3-/- thymi compared to controls at all time points analyzed (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of thymocyte numbers shown in Figure 1C with significance markers.

claim: There was no compensatory expression of kindlin-1 or kindlin-2 in kindlin-3-deficient thymi.
source: Importantly, we did not observe any compensatory expression of kindlin-1 or −2 in kindlin-3-deficient thymi (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing absence of kindlin-1 and kindlin-2 upregulation in Fermt3-/- thymi.

claim: Fermt3-/- thymi displayed normal cortico-medullary junctions at P3.
source: In line with the normal thymic cyto-architecture at P3, Fermt3-/- thymi displayed normal cortico-medullary junctions (CMJ) that separate CD4/CD8 DP T cells in the cortex from SP CD4 and CD8 T cells in the medulla, and normal epithelial meshes and vascular networks (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C demonstrating normal thymic architecture.

claim: At P6 and P8, the atrophic Fermt3-/- thymi showed a progressive enlargement of the medulla and a strong reduction of the cortex.
source: At P6 and P8, however, the atrophic Fermt3-/- thymi showed a progressive enlargement of the medulla and a strong reduction of the cortex suggesting an imbalanced development towards more mature SP T cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by H&E staining in Figure 1D showing altered thymic architecture at later time points.

claim: DN T cells were significantly reduced at P3 and P6 in Fermt3-/- thymi compared to controls.
source: This observation was confirmed by flow cytometry showing that DN T cells containing the most immature intrathymic T cells were significantly reduced at P3 and P6 in Fermt3-/- thymi compared to controls.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1E,F showing reduced DN cell frequencies.

claim: The relative distribution of DP and SP CD4 and CD8 T cells was comparable between WT and Fermt3-/- thymi at P3.
source: Notably, while the relative distribution of DP and SP CD4 and CD8 T cells was still comparable between WT and Fermt3-/- thymi at P3, the relative numbers of DP T cells decreased and SP CD4 and CD8 T cells increased in P6 thymi of Fermt3-/- mice (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1E showing similar percentages of DP and SP cells at P3.

claim: The relative numbers of DP T cells decreased and SP CD4 and CD8 T cells increased in P6 thymi of Fermt3-/- mice.
source: Notably, while the relative distribution of DP and SP CD4 and CD8 T cells was still comparable between WT and Fermt3-/- thymi at P3, the relative numbers of DP T cells decreased and SP CD4 and CD8 T cells increased in P6 thymi of Fermt3-/- mice (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1F showing altered percentages of DP and SP cells at P6.

claim: The absolute numbers of SP T cells were significantly reduced in P6 Fermt3-/- thymi compared to controls.
source: However, despite the shift towards SP T cell populations in P6 Fermt3-/- thymi, their absolute numbers were still significantly reduced compared to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E showing reduced absolute numbers of SP cells.

claim: The presence of normal relative SP T cell numbers in Fermt3-/- thymi until P3 suggests that intrathymic T cell differentiation proceeds independently of kindlin-3.
source: The presence of normal relative SP T cell numbers in Fermt3-/- thymi until P3 suggests that intrathymic T cell differentiation proceeds independently of kindlin-3.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that relative SP T cell numbers are normal at P3 despite kindlin-3 deficiency.

claim: DP and SP T cells from Fermt3-/- thymi show normal levels of T cell receptor (TCR), CD3 and costimulatory molecules such as CD5 and CD24.
source: This observation was supported by the normal levels of T cell receptor (TCR), CD3 and costimulatory molecules such as CD5 and CD24 on DP and SP T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F showing comparable expression levels of surface markers.

claim: Neither the number nor the frequency of apoptotic cells was altered in Fermt3-/- thymi at P3.
source: We found that neither the number (Figure 2C) nor the frequency (Figure 2D) of apoptotic cells (annexin V+/7-AAD-) was altered in Fermt3-/- thymi.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry data in Figure 2A-D showing no difference in apoptosis.

claim: Different T cell subsets isolated from WT and Fermt3-/- thymi showed comparable annexin V staining.
source: Furthermore, the different T cell subsets isolated from WT and Fermt3-/- thymi showed a comparable annexin V staining (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2E showing similar apoptosis levels across T cell subsets.

claim: There was a significantly reduced number of BrdU positive cells in P3 Fermt3-/- thymi both by immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry.
source: Next, we determined thymocyte proliferation by in vivo bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) labelling, which revealed a significantly reduced number of BrdU positive cells in P3 Fermt3-/- thymi both by immunohistochemistry (Figure 2F,H) and flow cytometry (Figure 2G,I).
evidence: Supported by BrdU incorporation data shown in Figure 2F-I demonstrating reduced proliferation.

claim: Reduced proliferation was detected in both the DP and the SP T cell populations in Fermt3-/- thymi.
source: Notably, reduced proliferation was detected in both the DP and the SP T cell populations (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2J showing reduced BrdU incorporation in DP and SP cells.

claim: Fermt3-/- T cells formed fewer contacts with DCs compared to control T cells.
source: Although Fermt3-/- T cells formed fewer contacts with DCs compared to control T cells, recruitment of LFA-1 and actin to the contact area as well as phospho-Tyrosine signals were indistinguishable between them suggesting that Fermt3-/- T cells form IS with DCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing immune synapse formation.

claim: Recruitment of LFA-1 and actin to the contact area as well as phospho-Tyrosine signals were indistinguishable between control and Fermt3-/- T cells.
source: Although Fermt3-/- T cells formed fewer contacts with DCs compared to control T cells, recruitment of LFA-1 and actin to the contact area as well as phospho-Tyrosine signals were indistinguishable between them suggesting that Fermt3-/- T cells form IS with DCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing normal molecular recruitment at immune synapses.

claim: A comparable proliferative response was observed when Fermt3-/- T cells were stimulated by DCs loaded with high concentration of MOG35-55 peptide or when a strong TCR signal was induced directly with anti-CD3/CD28 antibodies.
source: In line with the observation that Fermt3-/- T cells can form contacts with DCs, a comparable proliferative response was observed when these T cells were stimulated by DCs loaded with high concentration of MOG35-55 peptide or when a strong TCR signal was induced directly with anti-CD3/CD28 antibodies.
evidence: Supported by CFSE dilution assay data in Figure 2K showing normal proliferation under strong stimulation conditions.

claim: Fermt3-/- T cells failed to proliferate when dendritic cells were loaded with lower concentrations of MOG35-55 peptide.
source: In contrast, Fermt3-/- T cells failed to proliferate when dendritic cells were loaded with lower concentrations of MOG35-55 peptide (Figure 2K)
evidence: Supported by CFSE dilution assay data in Figure 2K showing impaired proliferation at low peptide concentrations.

claim: Defective integrin-mediated contact between kindlin-3-deficient T cells and APCs causes a reduced proliferative response contributing to thymus atrophy.
source: In contrast, Fermt3-/- T cells failed to proliferate when dendritic cells were loaded with lower concentrations of MOG35-55 peptide (Figure 2K) indicating that defective integrin-mediated contact between kindlin-3-deficient T cells and APCs causes a reduced proliferative response contributing to thymus atrophy of kindlin-3-deficient mice.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that Fermt3-/- T cells fail to proliferate under weak stimulation conditions.

claim: The reduced CD4 and CD8 DN T cell numbers in Fermt3-/- thymi point to an impaired T cell progenitor homing to the thymus.
source: The reduced CD4 and CD8 DN T cell numbers in Fermt3-/- thymi (Figure 1E,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E) point to an impaired T cell progenitor homing to the thymus.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation of reduced DN cell numbers.

claim: The Linneg DN population was significantly reduced in P3 and P6 thymi of Fermt3-/- mice.
source: These experiments revealed that the Linneg DN population was significantly reduced in P3 and P6 thymi and the DN1 and DN2 stage thymocytes were virtually absent from P3 Fermt3-/- thymi (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing reduced DN populations.

claim: DN1 and DN2 stage thymocytes were virtually absent from P3 Fermt3-/- thymi.
source: These experiments revealed that the Linneg DN population was significantly reduced in P3 and P6 thymi and the DN1 and DN2 stage thymocytes were virtually absent from P3 Fermt3-/- thymi (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing near absence of DN1 and DN2 cells.

claim: Circulating hematopoietic progenitor cells (Linneg, c-kit+, Sca-1- and Sca-1+) accumulate in the blood circulation of Fermt3-/- mice.
source: DN1 stage cells are the immediate intrathymic descendants of circulating hematopoietic progenitor cells (Linneg, c-kit+, Sca-1- and Sca-1+), which accumulate in the blood circulation of Fermt3-/- mice suggesting that extravasation of Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors is impaired (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3B,C showing increased circulating progenitors in Fermt3-/- mice.

claim: The accumulation of hematopoietic progenitor cells in the blood circulation of Fermt3-/- mice suggests that extravasation of Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors is impaired.
source: DN1 stage cells are the immediate intrathymic descendants of circulating hematopoietic progenitor cells (Linneg, c-kit+, Sca-1- and Sca-1+), which accumulate in the blood circulation of Fermt3-/- mice suggesting that extravasation of Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors is impaired (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Based on inference from the observation of progenitor accumulation in blood.

claim: The transfer of Fermt3-/- FL cells failed to reconstitute T cell development in the thymus of Rag2-/- recipient mice.
source: The transfer of Fermt3-/- FL cells failed to reconstitute T cell development in the thymus of Rag2-/- recipient mice (Figure 4A–C)
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4A-C showing lack of thymus reconstitution after Fermt3-/- FL cell transfer.

claim: Rag2-/- recipient thymi that received Fermt3-/- FL cells contained almost no DN1-2 cells.
source: The transfer of Fermt3-/- FL cells failed to reconstitute T cell development in the thymus of Rag2-/- recipient mice (Figure 4A–C), which also contained almost no DN1-2 cells (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4D,E showing near absence of DN1-2 cells.

claim: A very small number of Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors entered the Rag2-/- recipient thymus and differentiated into DN4 cells.
source: Interestingly, a very small number of Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors entered the Rag2-/- recipient thymus, differentiated into DN4 cells (Figure 4D,F)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4D,F showing presence of DN4 cells.

claim: Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors that entered the Rag2-/- recipient thymus produced a small number of circulating CD4 and CD8 T cells, which homed to the spleen.
source: Interestingly, a very small number of Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors entered the Rag2-/- recipient thymus, differentiated into DN4 cells (Figure 4D,F) and produced a small number of circulating CD4 and CD8 T cells, which homed to the spleen of Rag2-/- mice (Figure 4G–K)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4G-K showing presence of CD4 and CD8 T cells in blood and spleen.

claim: Kindlin-3 is very important for T cell progenitor homing to the adult thymus, but once in the thymus the progenitor cells differentiate into mature SP T cells that are released into the circulation.
source: Interestingly, a very small number of Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors entered the Rag2-/- recipient thymus, differentiated into DN4 cells (Figure 4D,F) and produced a small number of circulating CD4 and CD8 T cells, which homed to the spleen of Rag2-/- mice (Figure 4G–K) indicating that kindlin-3 is very important for T cell progenitor homing to the adult thymus, but once in the thymus the progenitor cells differentiate into mature SP T cells that are released into the circulation.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that a small number of Fermt3-/- progenitors can complete T cell development once they enter the thymus.

claim: Conditional deletion of Fermt3 by polyIC injection into Fermt3fl/fl/Mx1-Cre mice resulted in almost no DN (Linneg) cells in their thymi.
source: Since kindlin-3-deficient HSCs show an approximately 5-fold reduced homing capacity to the bone marrow, which might eventually impact on T cell progenitor generation (Ruppert et al., 2015), we conditionally deleted Fermt3 by injecting polyIC into Fermt3fl/fl/Mx1-Cre mice and detected almost no DN (Linneg) cells in their thymi, whereas control thymi from polyIC-treated Fermt3fl/fl mice clearly contained a discrete population of DN1-2 stage T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A showing loss of DN cells after conditional deletion.

claim: In mixed FL cell chimeras with 90% Fermt3-/- FL cells and 10% WT FL cells, only around 25% of the DN cells were of CD45.2 (Fermt3-/-) origin.
source: In addition, we generated mixed FL cell chimeras by transferring nine times more Fermt3-/- FL cells than WT FL cells into lethally irradiated recipient mice and compared their homing capacity to the thymus. To discriminate between both cell populations the WT FL cells were isolated from B6.SJL embryos, which express the CD45.1 allelic variant, while the Fermt3-/- embryos are from a C57BL/6 background expressing CD45.2. Despite the excess in transferred kindlin-3-deficient FL cells, only around 25% of the DN cells were of CD45.2 origin.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B showing disproportionate representation of Fermt3-/- cells.

claim: Chimeras made from 90% WT CD45.2 cells and 10% WT B6.SJL CD45.1 cells showed the 9:1 ratio in DN and all later T cell stages.
source: As a control, chimeras made from 90% WT CD45.2 cells and 10% WT B6.SJL CD45.1 cells showed the 9:1 ratio in DN and all later T cell stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B showing expected ratios in control chimeras.

claim: Only CD45+ leukocytes were EGFP-positive in thymi from Kindlin-3-EGFP knockin mice, while CD31+ endothelial cells and EPCAM+ thymic epithelial cells were EGFP negative.
source: Moreover, to exclude a defect in a non-hematopoietic cell type as cause for the Fermt3-/- T cell progenitor homing defect, we analysed thymi from Kindlin-3-EGFP knockin mice, which express kindlin-3 tagged C-terminally with EGFP. Flow cytometry of their thymi revealed that only CD45+ leukocytes were EGFP-positive and that CD31+ endothelial cells and EPCAM+ thymic epithelial cells were EGFP negative (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 showing cell-type specific kindlin-3 expression.

claim: The homing defect of kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors is of hematopoietic origin.
source: Altogether, these experiments show that kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors have a strong defect in homing to the postnatal and adult thymus and that the homing defect is of hematopoietic origin.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple experiments including conditional deletion, mixed chimeras, and kindlin-3-EGFP expression analysis.

claim: The first wave of WT CD45+ progenitor cells was observed within the perithymic mesenchyme at E11.5.
source: In line with previous reports (Douagi et al., 2000; Itoi et al., 2001), we observed the first wave of WT CD45+ progenitor cells within the perithymic mesenchyme at E11.5, and initial migration into the thymus primordium at E12.0 and scattering throughout the thymus at E12.5 and E13.5 (Figure 5A–F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5A-F and citations to previous studies (Douagi et al., 2000; Itoi et al., 2001).

claim: Fermt3-/- progenitor cells could be detected in the thymus primordium and the surrounding mesenchyme, however at lower numbers than WT.
source: Interestingly, also Fermt3-/- progenitor cells could be detected in the thymus primordium and the surrounding mesenchyme, however at lower numbers (Figure 5A–E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification in Figure 5A-E showing reduced but present Fermt3-/- progenitors.

claim: CD45+ progenitor cells accumulated at E13.5 in the Fermt3-/- thymus and continued developing into DN1-2 cells.
source: Despite the reduction, CD45+ progenitor cells accumulated at E13.5 in the Fermt3-/- thymus (Figure 5D) and continued developing into DN1-2 cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry data in Figure 5D,F showing progenitor accumulation and differentiation.

claim: A dramatic drop in the DN1-2 population was observed in Fermt3-/- thymi at E15-16.
source: Strikingly, a dramatic drop in the DN1-2 population was observed in Fermt3-/- thymi at E15-16 (Figure 5G,H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5G,H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B showing reduced DN1-2 cells at later embryonic stages.

claim: The absolute numbers of Linneg, c-kithi, CD45+, PIR+ T cell progenitors were comparable between WT and Fermt3-/- FLs.
source: The flow cytometric analyses revealed that the absolute numbers of Linneg, c-kithi, CD45+, PIR+ T cell progenitors were comparable between WT and Fermt3-/- FLs, while their frequency, due to a decreased cellularity of Fermt3-/- FLs, was increased (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6A-C showing similar absolute numbers of T cell progenitors in FL.

claim: The frequency of T cell progenitors in Fermt3-/- FLs was increased due to decreased cellularity of Fermt3-/- FLs.
source: The flow cytometric analyses revealed that the absolute numbers of Linneg, c-kithi, CD45+, PIR+ T cell progenitors were comparable between WT and Fermt3-/- FLs, while their frequency, due to a decreased cellularity of Fermt3-/- FLs, was increased (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6A-C showing increased frequency of progenitors.

claim: The numbers of circulating WT and Fermt3-/- Linneg, c-kithi, PIR+ T cell progenitors increased between E11.5 to E12.
source: The numbers of circulating WT and Fermt3-/- Linneg, c-kithi, PIR+ T cell progenitors increased between E11.5 to E12.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6D,E showing increased circulating progenitors at E12.

claim: The frequency of WT T cell progenitors steadily decreased between E12 and E13.5, while T cell progenitors accumulated in the circulation of Fermt3-/- fetuses.
source: However, while the frequency of WT T cell progenitors steadily decreased between E12 and E13.5, the T cell progenitors accumulated in the circulation of Fermt3-/- fetuses due to their reduced extravasation from pharyngeal vessels and/or impaired migration towards the thymus primordium (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6D,E showing differential kinetics of circulating progenitors.

claim: WT as well as Fermt3-/- FL cells moved persistently towards the thymic lobes in the thymus attraction assay.
source: Progenitor migration towards the thymic lobes was monitored for 36 to 48 hr by time-lapse video microscopy, which revealed that WT as well as Fermt3-/- FL cells moved persistently towards the thymic lobes, while migration was not induced when thymic lobes were absent (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data in Figure 7B showing directed migration of both WT and Fermt3-/- cells.

claim: CD45.2+ Fermt3-/- donor cells normally developed into DP, CD4 and CD8 SP cells in fetal thymus organ culture.
source: Consistent with our in vivo data, CD45.2+ Fermt3-/- donor cells normally developed into DP, CD4 and CD8 SP cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 7D showing normal T cell development in FTOC.

claim: Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors normally develop in the FL, are released into the circulation, sense the chemokine gradient, leave the pharyngeal vessel, migrate towards the thymus primordium, invade the thymus capsule and differentiate into different T cell subsets.
source: Altogether these findings indicate that Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors normally develop in the FL, are released into the circulation, sense the chemokine gradient, leave the pharyngeal vessel, albeit less efficiently than WT T cell progenitors, migrate towards the thymus primordium, invade the thymus capsule and differentiate into different T cell subsets.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple experimental observations including FL analysis, thymus attraction assay, and FTOC.

claim: The differential efficacy of Fermt3-/- T cell progenitor homing to the avascular and vascularized thymus was not due to different kindlin-3 and talin-1 protein levels in FL-derived and postnatal T progenitor cells.
source: The differential efficacy of Fermt3-/- T cell progenitor homing to the avascular and vascularized thymus was neither due to different kindlin-3 and talin-1 protein levels in lysates from sorted FL-derived T progenitor cells (Linneg, c-kit+, PIR+) isolated from E13.5 embryos and DN1 cells (Linneg, CD44+, CD25-) isolated from P6 thymi nor from an upregulation of talin-1 in Fermt3-/- PIR+ T cell progenitors (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 8A,B showing similar protein levels.

claim: Flow cytometry excluded differences in surface expression of α4, αL, β1, β2, β3 and β7 integrins on FL-derived T progenitor cells.
source: Flow cytometry also excluded differences in surface expression of α4, αL, β1, β2, β3 and β7 integrins on FL-derived T progenitor cells (Linneg, c-kit+, PIR+) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) and BM-derived LSK cells (Ruppert et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and citation to Ruppert et al., 2015.

claim: The CD31-positive vascular network was indistinguishable in E13.5 and E15.5 thymi from WT and Fermt3-/- mice.
source: Similarly, the CD31-positive vascular network was indistinguishable in E13.5 and E15.5 thymi from WT and Fermt3-/- mice excluding the possibility that a potential kindlin-3 expression in endothelial cells (Bialkowska et al., 2010) accounts for the defective homing to the vascularized thymus (data not shown).
evidence: Based on observation of normal vascular networks and citation to Bialkowska et al., 2010.

claim: VCAM-1, ICAM-1 and ICAM-2 expression was lower in pharyngeal vessels compared to intrathymic vessels.
source: Since adhesion and extravasation of Fermt3-/- T cells can occur on inflamed endothelium expressing high levels of VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 (Manevich-Mendelson et al., 2009; Moretti et al., 2013), we determined the expression of VCAM-1, ICAM-1 and ICAM-2 by immunostaining and flow cytometry and found them even lower expressed in pharyngeal vessels compared to intrathymic vessels.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry data in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A-E and citations to Manevich-Mendelson et al., 2009 and Moretti et al., 2013.

claim: Blood flow velocity and shear rates increased in the yolk sac vasculature between E12.5 to E16.5.
source: We therefore hypothesized that Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors show impaired adhesion to the vascular endothelium when blood flow velocity and shear forces increase during intrauterine development. To test this hypothesis, we injected red fluorescent microbeads into the yolk-sac vasculature of E12.5 to E16.5 embryos and measured blood flow velocity by intravital microscopy. We found an increase in blood flow velocity (Figure 8C) and shear rates (Figure 8D) between E12.5 to 16.5.
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy measurements shown in Figure 8C,D.

claim: Isolated T cell progenitors hardly adhered to P-selectin, CCL21/CCL25 and ICAM-1 in flow chamber assays.
source: Accordingly, in vitro flow chamber assays revealed that isolated T cell progenitors (Linneg, c-kit+, CD45+, Pir+) hardly adhered to P-selectin, CCL21/CCL25 and ICAM-1 (Figure 8E)
evidence: Supported by flow chamber assay data in Figure 8E showing minimal adhesion to ICAM-1.

claim: T cell progenitors readily adhered to P-selectin, CCL21/CCL25 and VCAM-1 in a shear stress-dependent manner.
source: Accordingly, in vitro flow chamber assays revealed that isolated T cell progenitors (Linneg, c-kit+, CD45+, Pir+) hardly adhered to P-selectin, CCL21/CCL25 and ICAM-1 (Figure 8E), while they readily adhered to P-selectin, CCL21/CCL25 and VCAM-1 in a shear stress-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by flow chamber assay data in Figure 8F showing adhesion to VCAM-1.

claim: Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors adhered to VCAM-1 but displayed a significantly reduced shear force resistance.
source: Interestingly, Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors adhered to VCAM-1 but displayed a significantly reduced shear force resistance (Figure 8F)
evidence: Supported by flow chamber assay data in Figure 8F showing detachment at higher shear rates.

claim: The increase in blood flow velocity and shear forces during fetal development prevents Fermt3-/- T cell progenitor adhesion and extravasation at intrathymic vessels.
source: Interestingly, Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors adhered to VCAM-1 but displayed a significantly reduced shear force resistance (Figure 8F) suggesting that the increase in blood flow velocity and shear forces during fetal development prevents Fermt3-/- T cell progenitor adhesion and extravasation at intrathymic vessels.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that Fermt3-/- progenitors cannot resist high shear forces and that shear forces increase during development.

claim: A reduced number of adherent Fermt3 hypomorphic T cells was observed in the LN vasculature compared to WT cells.
source: As expected, we observed a reduced number of adherent Fermt3 hypomorphic T cells in the LN vasculature compared to WT cells (Figure 8H,I).
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy data in Figure 8H,I showing reduced adhesion of hypomorphic cells.

claim: Fermt3 hypomorphic cells adhered preferentially in vessel segments where blood flow velocity and shear rates were lower compared to WT T cells.
source: We then injected fluorescent microspheres and measured the blood flow velocities in LN vessel segments and determined shear rates adherent cells were exposed to in those vessels. We found that Fermt3 hypomorphic cells adhered preferentially in vessel segments where blood flow velocity and shear rates were lower compared to WT T cells. The latter adhered to vessel segments with higher blood flow velocities and shear rates (Figure 8J,K).
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy measurements in Figure 8J,K showing differential adhesion based on shear rates.

claim: Kindlin-3 is crucial to stabilize integrin-mediated T cell adhesion to vessel walls exposed to high vascular shear forces.
source: These findings indicate that kindlin-3 is crucial to stabilize integrin-mediated T cell adhesion to vessel walls exposed to high vascular shear forces.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple experiments showing that cells with reduced kindlin-3 cannot adhere at high shear rates.

claim: In the absence of kindlin-3, a well-organized thymus with normal thymus architecture consisting of the four major compartments is initially formed.
source: We found that in the absence of kindlin-3 a well-organized thymus with normal thymus architecture consisting of the four major compartments (subcapsular zone, cortex, medulla and cortico-medullary junction) is initially formed.
evidence: Based on histological and immunofluorescence observations of thymic architecture.

claim: Chemokine-driven migration and positioning of developing T cells to specialized thymic microdomains is not impaired in the absence of kindlin-3.
source: The presence and clear separation of DP thymocytes in the cortex from SP CD4 and CD8 T cells in the medulla of postnatal thymi indicate that chemokine-driven migration and positioning of developing T cells to specialized thymic microdomains is not impaired in the absence of kindlin-3 allowing a well-orchestrated developmental maturation from T cell progenitors to mature T cells.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation of normal spatial organization of T cell subsets in Fermt3-/- thymi.

claim: Chemokine sensing and leukocyte migration within a 3D environment can occur in the absence of kindlin-3.
source: Thus, our data indicate that chemokine sensing and leukocyte migration within a 3D environment can occur in the absence of kindlin-3´s role to regulate integrin activity, which is in line with a previous report (Lämmermann et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on inference from observations of normal intrathymic migration and citation to Lämmermann et al., 2008.

claim: The thymi from kindlin-3 deficient mice began shrinking after birth.
source: While early thymic development is hardly affected by the lack of kindlin-3, the thymi from kindlin-3 deficient mice began shrinking after birth.
evidence: Based on observations of thymus size and cellularity over time.

claim: Kindlin-3-deficient thymocytes exhibited reduced proliferation rates due to a weakened interaction with thymic APCs.
source: We found two main reasons for the thymic atrophy. First, kindlin-3-deficient thymocytes exhibited reduced proliferation rates due to a weakened interaction with thymic APCs.
evidence: Based on BrdU incorporation assays and in vitro proliferation assays with DCs.

claim: A weakened interaction with APCs was reported for CD4 T cells isolated from LFA-1 and talin-1 knockout mice to cause reduced T cell proliferation.
source: A weakened interaction with APCs was also reported for CD4 T cells isolated from LFA-1 and talin-1 knockout mice to cause reduced T cell proliferation (Graf et al., 2007; Kandula and Abraham, 2004; Wernimont et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Graf et al., 2007; Kandula and Abraham, 2004; Wernimont et al., 2011.

claim: A severe T cell progenitor homing defect becomes apparent at the end of embryogenesis in kindlin-3-deficient mice.
source: Secondly, we observed a severe T cell progenitor homing defect, which becomes apparent at the end of embryogenesis.
evidence: Based on flow cytometry data showing dramatic reduction in DN1-2 cells at E15-16.

claim: FL-derived T cell progenitors start colonizing the thymus anlage at around embryonic day E11.5.
source: FL-derived T cell progenitors start colonizing the thymus anlage at around embryonic day (E) 11.5.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of T cell development and supported by immunofluorescence observations.

claim: The thymus anlage is initially avascular.
source: Since the thymus anlage is initially avascular, T cell progenitors exit the adjacent pharyngeal vessels, migrate towards the thymic primordium, cross the dense extracellular matrix of the thymic capsule and finally settle in the thymic tissue.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of thymus development.

claim: Kindlin-3-dependent adhesiveness through multiple integrin classes expressed on T lymphoid progenitors is essential for their homing to the vascularized thymus.
source: This process is critically dependent on kindlin-3. Furthermore, our findings also show that kindlin-3-dependent adhesiveness through multiple integrin classes expressed on T lymphoid progenitors is essential for their homing to the vascularized thymus, while loss of individual integrins either did not or only partially diminish precursor T cell homing (Scimone et al., 2006).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations and citation to Scimone et al., 2006.

claim: Loss of individual integrins either did not or only partially diminish precursor T cell homing.
source: Furthermore, our findings also show that kindlin-3-dependent adhesiveness through multiple integrin classes expressed on T lymphoid progenitors is essential for their homing to the vascularized thymus, while loss of individual integrins either did not or only partially diminish precursor T cell homing (Scimone et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Scimone et al., 2006.

claim: Kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors were able to colonize the non-vascularized thymus primordium and develop into SP CD4 and CD8 T cells that are released into the circulation and found in the spleen.
source: Our findings also revealed that kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors were able to colonize the non-vascularized thymus primordium and develop into SP CD4 and CD8 T cells that are released into the circulation and found in the spleen.
evidence: Based on observations from fetal thymus colonization studies and Rag2-/- chimera experiments.

claim: Early colonization of the thymus anlage was slightly delayed and less efficient in kindlin-3-deficient embryos.
source: Although early colonization of the thymus anlage was slightly delayed and less efficient, kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors were capable to leave the pharyngeal vessels and migrate through the mesenchymal tissue before they reach and enter the thymic anlage.
evidence: Based on immunofluorescence quantification showing reduced but present progenitors in early thymus.

claim: The reduced homing performance of kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors was not due to their reduced production in the FL and/or release into the circulation.
source: The reduced homing performance of kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors was neither due to their reduced production in the FL and/or release into the circulation, nor due to a defect in sensing chemokine cues that direct them towards the thymic primordium.
evidence: Based on flow cytometry data showing normal numbers of progenitors in FL and their release into circulation.

claim: The reduced homing performance of kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors was not due to a defect in sensing chemokine cues.
source: The reduced homing performance of kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors was neither due to their reduced production in the FL and/or release into the circulation, nor due to a defect in sensing chemokine cues that direct them towards the thymic primordium.
evidence: Based on thymus attraction assay showing normal chemotaxis of Fermt3-/- progenitors.

claim: Reduced adhesion to the pharyngeal vessel wall accounts for the mild T cell progenitor homing defect of kindlin-3-deficient embryos.
source: So, we assume that reduced adhesion to the pharyngeal vessel wall accounts for the mild T cell progenitor homing defect of kindlin-3-deficient embryos, an assumption, which is also supported by the accumulation of T cell progenitors in the embryonic circulation.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation of progenitor accumulation in fetal blood.

claim: FL-derived T cell progenitors are initially capable but later fail to home to the thymus, suggesting that cell extrinsic rather than cell intrinsic factors are responsible for the impaired colonization.
source: The fact that FL-derived T cell progenitors are initially capable but later fail to home to the thymus suggests that cell extrinsic rather than cell intrinsic factors are responsible for the impaired colonization.
evidence: Based on inference from the temporal pattern of homing defects.

claim: Kindlin-3-deficient thymi exhibited a dramatic drop in the number of DN1 and DN2 cells between E15 to E16, which is the time point when the thymus becomes vascularized.
source: Since kindlin-3-deficient thymi exhibited a dramatic drop in the number of DN1 and DN2 cells between E15 to E16, which is the time point when the thymus becomes vascularized (Liu et al., 2006), we suggest that differences in the adhesive properties of pharyngeal vs. intrathymic vessels account for this phenomenon.
evidence: Based on flow cytometry data and citation to Liu et al., 2006.

claim: Differences in the adhesive properties of pharyngeal vs. intrathymic vessels account for the differential homing capacity of kindlin-3-deficient progenitors.
source: Since kindlin-3-deficient thymi exhibited a dramatic drop in the number of DN1 and DN2 cells between E15 to E16, which is the time point when the thymus becomes vascularized (Liu et al., 2006), we suggest that differences in the adhesive properties of pharyngeal vs. intrathymic vessels account for this phenomenon.
evidence: Based on inference from temporal correlation between vascularization and homing defect.

claim: Kindlin-3-deficient effector T cells can leave the brain vascular system during inflammation when the endothelium expresses ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 at high levels.
source: In support of this hypothesis, we reported that kindlin-3-deficient effector T cells can leave the brain vascular system during inflammation when the endothelium expresses ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 at high levels (Moretti et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moretti et al., 2013.

claim: Kindlin-3-deficient effector T cells cannot extravasate from inflamed dermal microvessels but are able to leave postcapillary venules of skin-draining inflamed lymph nodes.
source: Similarly, kindlin-3-deficient effector T cells cannot extravasate from inflamed dermal microvessels but are able to leave postcapillary venules of skin-draining inflamed lymph nodes, probably because the high expression of integrin ligands and P-selectin stabilizes the weak adhesions of kindlin-3-deficient T cells (Cohen et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cohen et al., 2013.

claim: Kindlin-3 is important in stabilizing integrin-ligand interactions by promoting integrin clustering.
source: Beside its role in triggering integrin activation in association with talin-1 (Ma et al., 2008; Montanez et al., 2008; Moser et al., 2009a; Moser et al., 2009b; Moser et al., 2008), kindlin-3 is important in stabilizing integrin-ligand interactions by promoting integrin clustering (Feng et al., 2012; Ye et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Feng et al., 2012 and Ye et al., 2013.

claim: Low shear force conditions may allow adhesion of kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors to fetal pharyngeal microvessels, hence enabling their extravasation.
source: Thus, low shear force conditions may allow adhesion of kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors to fetal pharyngeal microvessels, hence enabling their extravasation.
evidence: Based on inference from flow chamber experiments and blood flow measurements.

claim: With increasing shear forces at later time points during fetal life, T cell progenitors lacking kindlin-3 are not able to efficiently adhere to and migrate out of microvessels into the thymus.
source: However with increasing shear forces at later time points during fetal life, T cell progenitors lacking kindlin-3 and therefore the ability to strengthening integrin-mediated adhesion are not able to efficiently adhere to and migrate out of microvessels into the thymus.
evidence: Based on inference from flow chamber experiments showing detachment at high shear and blood flow measurements showing increasing shear during development.

claim: High expression of α4β1 on the surface of FL-derived T cell progenitors supports the ability to resist low shear forces.
source: The ability to resist low shear forces is also supported by an early report that found high expression of α4β1 on the surface of FL-derived T cell progenitors (Kawakami et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kawakami et al., 1999.

claim: α4β1-mediated adhesiveness to VCAM-1 is less affected by loss of kindlin-3 in contrast to αLβ2 integrin-mediated adhesion to ICAM-1.
source: In addition, we and others have shown that α4β1-mediated adhesiveness to VCAM-1 is less affected by loss of kindlin-3 in contrast to αLβ2 integrin-mediated adhesion to ICAM-1 (Klapproth et al., 2015; Manevich-Mendelson et al., 2009; Moretti et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Klapproth et al., 2015; Manevich-Mendelson et al., 2009; Moretti et al., 2013.

claim: Lack of β1 integrin expression on hematopoietic stem cells abolishes their extravasation and homing to the BM.
source: In this respect, it is interesting to note that lack of β1 integrin expression on hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) abolishes their extravasation and homing to the BM (Potocnik et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citation to Potocnik et al., 2000.

claim: Kindlin-3-deficient HSCs revealed significantly diminished but not absent homing to the BM.
source: In this respect, it is interesting to note that lack of β1 integrin expression on hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) abolishes their extravasation and homing to the BM (Potocnik et al., 2000), whereas kindlin-3-deficient HSCs revealed significantly diminished but not absent homing to the BM (Ruppert et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ruppert et al., 2015.

claim: Kindlin-3 is dispensable for integrin-mediated T cell adhesion and signalling at low and indispensable at high vascular shear forces.
source: Taken together, our work demonstrates that kindlin-3 is dispensable for integrin-mediated T cell adhesion and signalling at low and indispensable at high vascular shear forces.
evidence: Based on synthesis of multiple experimental observations including flow chamber assays, blood flow measurements, and in vivo adhesion studies.

claim: This work shows a general, crucial role of integrins during T cell development.
source: Furthermore, we also show a general, crucial role of integrins during T cell development and suggest an additional not yet investigated T cell phenotype in LADIII patients.
evidence: Based on inference from the comprehensive analysis of integrin function via kindlin-3 deficiency.

claim: There may be an additional not yet investigated T cell phenotype in LADIII patients.
source: Furthermore, we also show a general, crucial role of integrins during T cell development and suggest an additional not yet investigated T cell phenotype in LADIII patients.
evidence: Based on speculation from the findings in mouse models.

claim: Loss of kindlin-3 impairs the functions of all integrins on hematopoietic cells studied so far.
source: Consequently, loss of kindlin-3 impairs the functions of all integrins on hematopoietic cells studied so far and leads to severe defects affecting platelets, leukocytes, osteoclasts and hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) (Krüger et al., 2008; Moser et al., 2009a; Moser et al., 2008; Ruppert et al., 2015; Schmidt et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies (Krüger et al., 2008; Moser et al., 2009a; Moser et al., 2008; Ruppert et al., 2015; Schmidt et al., 2011).

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in the human KINDLIN-3/FERMT3 gene cause leukocyte adhesion deficiency type-III (LAD-III) syndrome.
source: In line with genetic studies in mice, loss-of-function mutations in the human KINDLIN-3/FERMT3 gene cause leukocyte adhesion deficiency type-III (LAD-III) syndrome, which is characterized by severe bleedings, infections and accumulation of HSPCs in the blood circulation (Kuijpers et al., 2009; Malinin et al., 2009; Mory et al., 2008; Ruppert et al., 2015; Svensson et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies (Kuijpers et al., 2009; Malinin et al., 2009; Mory et al., 2008; Ruppert et al., 2015; Svensson et al., 2009).

claim: LAD-III syndrome is characterized by severe bleedings, infections and accumulation of HSPCs in the blood circulation.
source: In line with genetic studies in mice, loss-of-function mutations in the human KINDLIN-3/FERMT3 gene cause leukocyte adhesion deficiency type-III (LAD-III) syndrome, which is characterized by severe bleedings, infections and accumulation of HSPCs in the blood circulation (Kuijpers et al., 2009; Malinin et al., 2009; Mory et al., 2008; Ruppert et al., 2015; Svensson et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical studies (Kuijpers et al., 2009; Malinin et al., 2009; Mory et al., 2008; Ruppert et al., 2015; Svensson et al., 2009).
